units.title: The Scientific Revolution and The Enlightenment

cards.title: The Scientific Revolution
body: In the Middle Ages, many educated Europeans became more interested in the world around them, but their knowledge was based on the ides of ancient philosophers instead of reason and observation. But several changes in the 15th-16th C encouraged the Medieval philosophers abandon their old views and develop new ones, such as

Renaissance humanists began to master Greek and the works of Ptolemy, Archimedes and Plato. They realized that those philosophers didn’t agree with Aristotle but had similar ideas with the Medieval thinkers.
Technical problems and calculations become easier with the invention of new instruments such the telescope and microscope.
The printing press helped spread new ideas quickly followed by the rediscovery of ancient mathematics.

cards.title: A Revolution in Astronomy
body: Medieval Astronomical discoveries completely changed the existing concept of the universe.

Ptolemy was a great Astronomer of the 2ndC whose ideas along with that of Aristotle and the Christian view were later put in the Ptolemic System. This system believes in the Geocentric view of the Universe where the Earth was the center of the Universe and the Sun revolved around it.

In May 1543, Nicholas Copernicus, a mathematician, believed in the Heliocentric view where the Sun was at the center of the Universe and the Earth revolved around it just as the moon revolves around the planets.
Johannes Kepler came up with studies of planetary motion and supported the Heliocentric view.

Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist who provided the answers for, what planets are made of? and the motion of the Universe by inventing the Telescope. Using the telescope, Galileo discovered mountains on the moon, moons revolving around Jupiter and sunspots. He also discovered that all planets were composed of material substances instead of pure orbs of light, according to the Ptolemc system.

The Copernican ideas were rejected by the Catholic church as they shook the Christian ideas. Galileo was arrested by the church and was forced to retrack his ideas. Giordano Bruno was another Italian philosopher who was burned on the stake by the church for his beliefs of infinite universe.
Isaac Newton was a philosopher and a mathematician, who wrote the 3 laws of motion and the force of gravity.

cards.title: Developments in Medicine and Chemistry, 16thC
body: Andreas Vesalius who wrote ‘On the Fabric of the Human Body’ written in 1543, he came up with human anatomy based on conducting accurate examinations on the individual Human organs. But like the past mistakes he believed in the two kinds of blood flowing in the veins and arteries.
William Harvey wrote ‘On the Motion of the Heart and Blood’ in 1628, proved that the same blood flowed I the veins and the arteries.

Robert Boyle was one of the first scientists to conduct controlled experiments on the properties of gases leading to Boyle’s Law. He believed that the volume of gases varies with the pressure exerted on them.
Antoine Lavoisier invented a system of naming the chemical elements, much of which is still used today. He is regarded by many as the founder of modern chemistry.

cards.title: Philosophies
body: Rene Descartes was a French modern rationalist who emphasized on doubt and uncertainty. He talked of the importance of the mind and that he would only accept as true only those things that he can reason out. Descartes has been called the father of modern rationalism. According to Descartes reason is the chief source of knowledge.

“I think therefore I am” is one of the most famous philosophical quotes influenced by Western Philosophy. The quote was used by Descartes to answer the question what warrants the declaration of existence?

cards.title: Women in the Scientific Revolution
body: Margaret Cavendish was a British scientist who wrote a book about experimental philosophy. In Germany 14% of the astronomers were women.

cards.title: The Scientific Method
body: Francis Bacon was a British scientist who believed in experiment and reasoning to learn about nature by conducting systemic observations and carefully organized experiments to test hypotheses to come up with correct principles. Bacon wanted to employ science in industry, agriculture and trade.

cards.title: the Enlightenment
body: The Enlightenment was an 18thC intellectual movement of philosophers who were greatly impressed with the achievements of the Scientific Revolution. One of the favorite words of these intellectuals was reason, which meant the application of the scientific method to an understanding of all life.
The Enlightenment was especially influenced by the ideas of two 17thC Englishmen, Isaac Newton and John Locke.

Isaac Newton was an English Scientist who saw the physical world and everything in it as a giant machine (the Newtonian world-machine). The intellectuals of the Enlightenment thought they could discover the natural laws that governed human society.
Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) was a French scientist, one of the most influential writers of the French Renaissance he introduced ‘essay’ as new literary genre and the founder of modern skepticism.

John Locke suggested that people were molded by the experiences that came through their senses from the surrounding world. If environments were changed and people were exposed to the right influences, then people could be changed, and a new society would be created.

cards.title: Enlightenment Thinkers and Their Ideas
body: Most of the thinkers of the Enlightenment were French, but some English philosophers.

Montesquieu-his full name was Charles-Louis de Secondat, the Baron de Montesquieu, came from the French nobility. His most famous work ‘The Spirit of the Laws’ was published in 1748. In this study of governments, Montesquieu identified three branches the executive, the legislative (parliament) and judiciary (the court of law).

Voltaire- his real name was François-Marie Arouet, known simply as Voltaire by his pen name. Voltaire was especially well known for his criticism of Christianity and his strong belief in religious tolerance. He strongly advocated against religious intolerance in France.
Denis Diderot is the writer of the Encyclopedia, or Classified Dictionary. Published between 1751 and 1772, the Encyclopedia attacked religious superstition and supported religious toleration.

David Hume (1711–1776), was a Scottish philosopher, historian, economist, and writer known especially for his philosophical empiricism and skepticism. He was one of the most important figures in the history of Enlightenment. ‘A Treatise of Human Nature’ and ‘Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion’ are some of his influential works.

Adam Smith was a Scottish philosopher who founded the modern social science of economics. He believed that if individuals were free to pursue their own economic self-interest, all society would eventually benefit thus, the state should not interfere in the economy. This doctrine became known as laissez-faire, a French term meaning to let people do what they want.

cards.title: The Later Enlightenment (1760s)
body: Jean-Jacques Rousseau presented his concept of the Social Contract, published in 1762. Through a social contract, an entire society agrees to be governed by its general will. Individuals who wish instead to follow their own self-interest must be forced to abide by the general will. Thus, liberty is achieved by being forced to follow what is best for “the general will,” because the general will represents what is best for the entire community.

For centuries, male thinkers had argued that the nature of women made them inferior to men and made male domination of women necessary. By the eighteenth century, however, female thinkers began to express their ideas about improving the condition of women.

Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer who wrote ‘In A Vindication of the Rights of Women’, she argued that the domination of men over women was wrong and that the Enlightenment was based on an ideal of reason in all human beings. Because women have reason, then they are entitled to the same rights as men. She advocated for women’s equal rights in education, as well as in economic and political life.

cards.title: The Social World of the Enlightenment
body: The Enlightenment was not a movement belonging exclusively to the nobles and aristocrats. For example, enlightenment thinkers such as Diderot and Rousseau came from the lower middle class. The movement, however, greatly influenced the aristocrats and upper classes in the larger cities. The common people, especially the peasants, were mostly unaware and little affected by the Enlightenment.

The Salon- Salons were the elegant drawing rooms of the wealthy upper class. Invited guests gathered in these salons and took part in conversations that discussed the new ideas of the philosophe and helped the spread of Enlightenment ideas. Hosts of the salons were mostly wealthy upper-class women.

cards.title: Religion and the Enlightenment
body: It was a period of reason vs dogma the period gave the rise of three ideas to question the existence of God, Deism (reason), Agnosticism (to question existence of God) it brought to the idea of atheism denial of God known as Atheism.

lessons.title: Political Ideas and European Politics in the Age of the Enlightenment Political ideas

cards.title: A. Political Ideas
body: Enlightenment writers believed in natural rights for all people, rights such as; equality before the law, freedom of religious worship, freedom of speech, freedom of the press, and the rights to assemble, hold property, and pursue happiness. These rulers must allow religious freedom, freedom of speech and of the press, and the rights of private property, obey the laws and enforce them fairly for all subjects. Enlightenment influenced both the American and French revolutions.

cards.title: B. War of the Austrian Succession (1740-1748)
body: The war started when Maria Theresa succeeded Charles VI as the queen of Austria. King Frederick II of Prussia took the advantage of the succession to invade Austria and he seized Silesia. France joined the war on the side of Prussia, while Britain entered the war on the side of Austria.

The war was fought in Europe, the Far East and North America and only ended with the treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle in 1748. Since all parties were exhausted after seven years of warfare, they agreed to the treaty.

cards.title: C, The Seven Years War (1756-1763)
body: After Prussia refused to hand over Silesia, Maria won a revolutionary diplomacy with France by separating it from Prussia in 1756 and built an army. Thus, the old rivalry replaced by the French-British rivalry over colonial empires and Austria-Prussia over Silesia.

The war started when the alliance of France, Austria and Russia saw Prussia as threat, the British on the other hand allied with Prussia. The war had three major areas of conflict Europe, North America and India in 1756-1763.
The war ended 1763 and all occupied territories were returned to their original owners, the effects include;
France left India to the British by the treaty of Paris
Austria recognized permanent control of Silesia by Prussia
France gave Canada and Mississippi to England.
French gave French Louisiana to Spain.
Spain gave Spanish Florida to England.
By 1763 British become the strongest power in the world.
